slides.title: Solitary pandas exchange information through scent
body: Giant pandas, _Ailuropoda melanoleuca_, live largely apart, yet neighboring animals can use the same scent-marking sites. **Chemical communication** occurs when substances deposited by one animal influence another animal's behavior. A marked tree can retain information after the sender leaves.

Camera traps in Wolong recorded gland marking, urine marking, and subsequent olfactory investigation at the same site. These actions connect signal production with active sampling by a receiver, rather than requiring the two pandas to meet face to face.

Controlled odor presentations complement these field observations. Pandas repeatedly inspected conspecific scents and changed their investigation after encountering a different donor's secretion. Persistent environmental odors therefore support social assessment within a largely solitary lifestyle.

slides.title: Gland secretions and urine mix at shared marking sites
body: **Anogenital gland secretions** are substances released from glands near the anus and genital region. Pandas place these secretions on surfaces by rubbing the gland area against them. Urine provides another source of chemical information at many of the same locations.

Hou and colleagues sampled marked tree bark during the mating season in Wolong. Camera recordings documented different deposition postures at a shared tree, including gland contact and raised urine marking. The receiver encounters the resulting surface mixture.

Laboratory odor tests can separate urine from gland secretions, whereas wild bark contains their combined products plus environmental contributions. This difference connects a controlled response to a single scent type with the richer chemical substrate encountered during natural social investigation.

slides.title: Olfactory receptors span the membrane seven times
body: An **olfactory receptor** is a membrane protein involved in detecting odor molecules. Mammalian olfactory receptors belong to the G protein-coupled receptor family, whose proteins cross the cell membrane seven times and communicate with intracellular signaling proteins.

Zhou and colleagues searched the chromosome-level panda genome for receptor sequences and predicted their structural features. Transmembrane helices, segments that pass through the membrane, were among the features used to characterize these receptor proteins.

Receptor diversity provides a molecular basis for recognizing chemically varied stimuli. A single odor molecule can interact with several receptor types, and a receptor can respond to several molecules. Odor identity consequently depends on combinations of receptor interactions rather than one receptor representing one social message.

slides.title: The receptor repertoire contains intact and disrupted genes
body: The panda genome search identified 639 olfactory receptor sequences. Of these, 408 were classified as functional genes, 94 as partial genes, and 137 as **pseudogenes**, sequences disrupted by premature stop codons or shifts in the reading frame.

A reading frame determines how groups of nucleotide bases encode amino acids. A frameshift changes those groups, while a premature stop interrupts protein synthesis. The authors used these sequence features to distinguish disrupted genes from predicted full-length receptor genes.

The intact repertoire retains many potential receptor proteins despite the panda's specialized bamboo diet. Its mixture of conserved receptors and disrupted sequences records evolutionary change within the sensory system. Genomic classification identifies candidate proteins for testing how pandas detect food odors and social secretions.

slides.title: Class II receptors dominate the panda repertoire
body: A **phylogenetic tree** groups sequences according to their evolutionary relationships. Zhou and colleagues compared panda receptor proteins and assigned 345 functional sequences to Class II and 63 to Class I.

Class I and Class II are major evolutionary branches of vertebrate olfactory receptors. Class II receptors are particularly prominent in terrestrial mammals, whose olfactory systems sample molecules carried in air. The panda's receptor repertoire shares this terrestrial organization.

A scent mark contains multiple volatile compounds, molecules capable of entering the surrounding air. The predominance of Class II sequences is consistent with this chemical environment. Receptor class describes evolutionary affinity; precise sensitivity to a panda scent compound requires an odor-response measurement.

slides.title: Receptor genes occupy clusters across chromosomes
body: A **chromosome** is a long DNA molecule carrying genes. Functional olfactory receptor genes in the panda occur at multiple chromosomal locations, often in neighboring groups. Such a group is a gene cluster, rather than a distinct brain region.

Zhou and colleagues mapped receptor positions using the chromosome-level assembly. Among the chromosomally assigned sequences, chromosomes 8 and 16 contained especially dense receptor distributions. The map preserves both gene position and chromosome scale in megabases, where 1 megabase is one million DNA bases.

Clustered organization provides genomic context for receptor diversification. Related receptors can occupy neighboring positions while differing in protein sequence. This distributed gene inventory supports a diverse sensory repertoire through changes in genes, not through a single chromosome acting as an odor detector.

slides.title: Pandas retain shared and lineage-specific receptor families
body: A receptor **gene family** groups related sequences that descended from common ancestral genes. Zhou and colleagues clustered receptor proteins from pandas and other bears according to amino acid similarity, comparing shared groups with groups restricted to particular lineages.

The panda retained many receptor clusters shared with other bears and also had 31 clusters classified as unique in this comparison. Thus, dietary specialization coexists with both conserved and lineage-specific elements of the olfactory repertoire.

Shared sequences can preserve common molecular functions, while sequence divergence provides candidates for changed odor recognition. The observed combination supports studying both general bear olfaction and panda-specific chemical ecology. A lineage-specific sequence cluster is a genetic category, rather than proof of a receptor for a particular reproductive signal.

slides.title: Conserved motifs preserve receptor protein organization
body: A **motif** is a recurring pattern within a protein sequence. Conserved motifs remain similar across related species, suggesting that these portions of the protein retain constraints associated with their molecular organization.

Zhou and colleagues identified five strongly conserved motifs in functional olfactory receptor proteins across six bear species. Their sequence analysis also predicted an N-linked glycosylation site, a location where a sugar group can be attached to an asparagine residue.

These shared features occur alongside variation in receptor number and sequence. Panda specialization therefore involves changes within a recognizable mammalian receptor architecture. Conserved protein regions maintain similarities across the family, while more variable regions supply molecular diversity relevant to recognizing a broad mixture of environmental odors.

slides.title: Human receptor matches generate testable odor hypotheses
body: **Sequence homology** is similarity arising from shared ancestry. Zhou and colleagues compared panda receptor proteins with human receptors whose responses to odor molecules had been studied. Some panda sequences were similar enough to suggest candidate odor sensitivities.

These comparisons generate hypotheses about ligand recognition, where a ligand is a molecule that interacts with a receptor. The hypothesis is that related receptor sequences may recognize similar molecules; direct panda receptor assays are required to assign a particular ligand.

This distinction matters for scent chemistry. Hou and colleagues detected compounds such as nonanal and vanillin at wild marking sites. Detecting a compound in a mark and finding a related receptor sequence are complementary observations. They provide candidates for connecting signal chemistry with sensory responses.

slides.title: Serial sections reveal the panda olfactory forebrain
body: **Histology** examines tissue structure in thin sections. Lauer studied an adult female panda brain using 30 µm sections, with alternating stains for cell bodies and fiber tracts. This preparation distinguished neuronal groups from the pathways passing among them.

Cresyl violet emphasized cellular organization, while the Weil stain emphasized nerve fibers. Serial sections allowed the position and continuity of a structure to be followed from the front of the forebrain toward its posterior regions.

The study identified a differentiated anterior olfactory nucleus, olfactory tubercle, septal nuclei, and amygdaloid subdivisions. These structures establish anatomical locations for studying chemical sensory processing. Their boundaries are based on cell arrangement and fiber relationships within the panda brain, rather than behavioral labels assigned to a single undivided olfactory center.

slides.title: The anterior olfactory nucleus surrounds a ventricle
body: The **anterior olfactory nucleus** is a forebrain neuronal group located along the olfactory crus, the stalk connecting the bulb region with the hemisphere. In the panda, its cells form a ring around the olfactory ventricle, a fluid-containing cavity.

Lauer followed this ring through serial sections and distinguished dorsal, lateral, ventral, and medial portions. Their relative positions change as the crus joins the hemisphere. The medial portion was less developed than the other major divisions.

The organization is spatially continuous rather than a set of isolated points. Different sectors of the ring relate to different parts of the basal forebrain as the sections proceed posteriorly. This arrangement gives a concrete anatomical framework for tracing olfactory information beyond the bulb.

slides.title: Olfactory nuclear sectors merge with forebrain gray matter
body: **Gray matter** contains neuronal cell bodies and their local processes. Lauer found that the different sectors of the anterior olfactory nucleus continue into neighboring forebrain gray matter as the olfactory crus becomes attached to the hemisphere.

The lateral sector becomes continuous with prepyriform cortex, an anterior part of olfactory cortex. The ventral sector merges with the olfactory tubercle, while the medial sector relates to the anterior continuation of the hippocampal formation.

These transitions connect an anterior ring of neurons with several forebrain territories. A posterior nuclear portion becomes especially prominent near the ventricle and grades into deeper tubercular tissue. Serial histology therefore resolves an organized set of anatomical continuities that a surface view of the brain would conceal.

slides.title: The olfactory tubercle contains three cellular layers
body: The **olfactory tubercle** is a layered region of the basal forebrain located behind the anterior olfactory nucleus. Lauer distinguished a superficial plexiform layer, a pyramidal-cell layer, and a deeper polymorph layer in the panda.

A plexiform layer is rich in interwoven neuronal processes. Pyramidal cells have a roughly triangular cell body, while the polymorph layer contains cells of varied shapes. Their different arrangements make the layers identifiable in stained sections.

The intermediate tubercular region was particularly well differentiated. Its superficial layer contained many fibers associated with the lateral olfactory tract, while the deeper layer merged with anterior olfactory nuclear tissue. The layered organization places incoming fiber bundles beside organized neuronal populations within the same olfactory forebrain territory.

slides.title: The lateral olfactory tract borders layered forebrain tissue
body: The **lateral olfactory tract** is a bundle of nerve fibers associated with olfactory forebrain pathways. Lauer's panda sections place it beside the olfactory tubercle and the lateral portion of the anterior olfactory nucleus.

The lateral part of the tubercle bends inward over the tract. Its pyramidal layer contains many pyramidal cells, while its deeper polymorph layer broadens toward the claustrum and putamen, neighboring forebrain structures identified by their cellular architecture.

This geometry places a fiber route next to several distinct gray-matter territories. In the intermediate tubercle, fibers from the ventral part of the tract contribute substantially to the superficial plexiform layer. Anatomical relationships thus distinguish an axonal pathway from the neuronal layers positioned along it.

slides.title: Septal and accumbens territories border olfactory tissue
body: The **septum** is a medial forebrain region containing several neuronal groups. In Lauer's panda material, the lateral septal nucleus was the largest of the septal nuclei and lay near the lateral ventricle and anterior hippocampal continuation.

The **nucleus accumbens** occupies neighboring ventral tissue. The ventral lateral septal population merged with accumbens rostrally and with commissural and stria terminalis bed nuclei farther posteriorly. These changing relationships distinguish adjacent populations along the brain's front-to-back axis.

The olfactory tubercle also approached the accumbens and caudate nucleus along its deeper margin. This arrangement places olfactory-related tissue within a differentiated basal forebrain, rather than outside it as a separate sensory appendage. Cell density and shape provide landmarks for resolving these regional boundaries.

slides.title: The panda amygdala contains differentiated nuclear groups
body: The **amygdala** is a collection of forebrain nuclei rather than one homogeneous structure. Lauer described cortico-medial and baso-lateral groups in the panda, distinguishing them through their cell populations, location, and neighboring fiber bundles.

The medial and cortical nuclei occupy more medial and ventral positions, while basal and lateral nuclei occupy much of the lateral portion. A central nucleus lies dorsally through the posterior part of the complex.

The lateral nucleus was the largest and most extensive cell mass of the panda amygdaloid complex. The cortical nucleus was also particularly well developed. This differentiated organization supplies multiple anatomical territories for future studies relating chemical information to behavior, instead of treating all amygdaloid cells as equivalent.

The lateral nucleus was the largest and most extensive cell mass of the panda amygdaloid complex. The cortical nucleus was also particularly well developed. This differentiated organization supplies multiple anatomical territories for future studies relating chemical information to behavior, instead of treating all amygdaloid cells as equivalent.

Cortico-medial and baso-lateral name groups of nuclei, not single cell types. The names summarize the positions and relationships of subdivisions. Lauer compared this organization with other mammals and noted especially substantial development of the panda's baso-lateral group.

slides.title: Basal and lateral amygdaloid nuclei have distinct structure
body: The **basal amygdaloid nucleus** occupies a central position within the amygdaloid complex. Lauer separated it into large-celled and small-celled portions in the panda, with the large-celled portion directly dorsal to the small-celled portion.

The lateral nucleus lies lateral and dorsolateral to the basal nucleus. Fibers related to the external capsule, a neighboring white-matter bundle, divide parts of its projecting cell mass into smaller islands. These boundaries connect cellular organization with fiber architecture.

Posteriorly, the lateral nucleus approaches the hippocampus but is separated from it by the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. A smaller accessory basal nucleus also accompanies the basal nucleus. The arrangement resolves several distinct neuronal populations within tissue that would otherwise be described broadly as amygdala.

slides.title: Cortical amygdaloid tissue adjoins olfactory cortex
body: The **cortical amygdaloid nucleus** lies along the ventral part of the panda amygdaloid complex. Lauer identified its relatively dense superficial layer of pyramidal cells and its close relationship with neighboring olfactory cortical tissue.

A cortico-amygdaloid transition area contains mixed cell populations between pyriform cortex, the cortical nucleus, and the baso-lateral nuclear group. This transition is relatively broad in the panda sections and lacks sharp boundaries with several neighboring territories.

The central and medial nuclei remain distinguishable through their positions and associated fibers. slides.title: Close inspection samples odors from marked surfaces
body: **Chemosensory investigation** is active sampling of a chemical stimulus. In Swaisgood and colleagues' experiment, an investigation bout involved the panda bringing its nose within 5 cm of the odor board and sniffing.

Fresh female urine and male gland marks were transferred onto fir boards. Observers measured investigation during 10-minute tests and checked records against video. The animal could sniff, lick, manipulate the board, or rub the scent onto its fur.

Pandas often inspected a detected scent intensely even after previously passing nearby. This response separates close assessment from simple movement toward an odor source. The wild camera records likewise document surface investigation at marked trees, connecting the experimental measurement with a natural action performed at communication sites.

slides.title: Unscented boards isolate the response to conspecific odor
body: A **control stimulus** preserves features of the preparation while omitting the factor being tested. Swaisgood and colleagues presented unscented fir boards because fir itself has an odor and the board was part of every experimental presentation.

Control boards were rubbed on surfaces inaccessible to panda contact. Pandas spent little time investigating them compared with boards carrying urine or gland secretion. Flehmen responses also occurred with conspecific scents but were absent from the control presentations.

These comparisons locate the sustained response in the added animal-derived material. The board served as a transportable substrate, while the scent provided the biologically salient component. Matching the substrate permits a chemical communication experiment to distinguish responses to conspecific information from responses to the wooden test object.

slides.title: Repeated donor odor produces habituation
body: **Habituation** is a reduction in response after repeated exposure to a stimulus. Pandas received scent from the same donor on five consecutive days. Their investigation generally declined across these presentations, with especially clear decreases for male gland secretions.

The repeated samples were freshly collected rather than one unchanged object being presented each day. Declining investigation therefore occurred despite continuing exposure to new samples carrying the same donor's odor characteristics.

On the sixth day, the investigators presented familiar and novel donor scents together. Positions were randomized, and the two boards were separated by approximately 0.3 m. This design tests whether the reduction in investigation is specific enough for another donor's chemical profile to renew sampling.

slides.title: Male gland odors support individual discrimination
body: **Individual discrimination** occurs when an animal responds differently to cues from different individuals. After habituation, both male and female pandas investigated a novel male's gland secretion more than the familiar male's secretion.

The donors in a discrimination test were the same sex, and both stimuli were gland secretions. Thus, the comparison depended on differences between male odor profiles rather than a switch between sexes or between urine and gland material.

The renewed investigation means that male gland secretions contain information that distinguishes donors. The behavioral result establishes perceptual discrimination of individual odors. Associating each odor with the identity of a previously encountered animal would require a separate recognition task, because these two forms of performance involve different information.

slides.title: Urine and gland signals differ in discrimination strength
body: Female urine and male gland secretions produced different discrimination patterns in the same habituation protocol. **Signal salience** refers to how strongly a stimulus attracts or guides a receiver's response in a particular task.

Responses to male gland odors gave clear evidence of donor discrimination in both sexes. Female urine produced a tendency toward greater novel-odor investigation, but the urine tests gave weaker evidence of discrimination. The two materials therefore supported different levels of behavioral differentiation under these conditions.

The comparison combines donor sex with material type: female donors supplied urine, while male donors supplied gland secretions. Consequently, the difference cannot be attributed solely to sex. The clear gland result and weaker urine result describe the tested signals, while identifying urine chemistry requires a matched-material comparison.

slides.title: Flehmen accompanies renewed chemical assessment
body: **Flehmen** is a chemosensory behavior involving deep inhalation, an upward movement of the head, and a slight curl of the upper lip. Panda odor experiments recorded it separately from the duration of ordinary sniffing.

In the individual-discrimination study, flehmen occurred more readily with novel male gland odors than with the familiar gland odors. Unscented control boards failed to elicit it. The response therefore changed with the chemical stimulus and its recent familiarity.

Height experiments also found more flehmen toward elevated urine and gland marks. Together, these results connect a distinct sampling behavior with both donor novelty and the physical placement of a signal. Counting flehmen and measuring sniffing provide complementary descriptions of how pandas actively assess conspecific chemical information.

slides.title: Scent height changes responses to identical male urine
body: A panda's marking posture determines where its chemical material reaches a surface. White and colleagues tested male urine at 0.0 m and 1.0 m, approximating a ground-level squat and an elevated handstand mark.

Each urine sample was divided into two 10 mL portions, preserving the donor and chemical composition across the height comparison. The researchers changed placement rather than replacing the odor with material from another male.

Pandas investigated the high urine longer and performed more flehmen after encountering it. Because observations began after the animal first sampled the stimulus, the response concerned assessment following detection. Spatial context therefore changed the value assigned to an otherwise matched chemical stimulus, extending communication beyond the molecules alone.

slides.title: Elevated gland marks attract longer investigation
body: White and colleagues placed matched **gland marks** at ground level or 0.5 m, approximating squat and reverse or legcock marking. These comparisons were conducted separately for male and female donor secretions.

Pandas spent longer investigating elevated marks from both sexes. They also performed more flehmen toward high male gland marks, while high female gland marks elicited more flehmen in most receiver categories.

The height effect therefore extended beyond male urine. A secretion's location contributed to how it was assessed even when its donor and material remained constant. Male and female gland odors produced overlapping effects on sampling, but their subsequent behavioral consequences differed, connecting a shared sensory response with signal-specific social actions.

slides.title: High male urine shifts subsequent spatial behavior
body: **Avoidance** can be measured as greater distance from a stimulus after it is encountered. White and colleagues recorded the panda's position once per minute during the observation session, linking scent sampling with later movement within the enclosure.

Pandas remained farther from male urine placed at 1.0 m than from the matched ground-level urine. The pattern was particularly pronounced in subadult males. Longer initial investigation therefore coexisted with greater subsequent distance.

The authors proposed the hypothesis that elevated male urine signals competitive ability or readiness to escalate. The observed spatial response is consistent with assessing a potentially consequential rival. Sampling a signal and remaining near its source are distinct behavioral outcomes, so greater investigation need not indicate attraction to the marked location.

slides.title: Receiver age changes the intensity of scent assessment
body: A **subadult** is an animal that has not yet reached full adult status. White and colleagues compared adult and subadult receivers, making developmental state part of the chemical communication experiment rather than treating every panda as an equivalent observer.

Subadults investigated male urine longer, displayed more flehmen, and investigated their surroundings more often than adults. Subadults also spent longer investigating male gland secretions. These age effects concerned responses to adult male donor material.

Responses to female gland material showed a different pattern, with no overall age effect on investigation or flehmen. Developmental state therefore interacted with the type of social information sampled. Height and receiver age both influenced assessment, but they represented different factors: signal placement and the condition of the animal receiving it.

body: **Environmental investigation** is sniffing directed toward the surroundings rather than toward the experimentally placed scent. White and colleagues recorded it as a separate behavioral category, alongside stimulus sniffing, flehmen, licking, marking, and distance.

After exposure to elevated female gland secretions, pandas performed more bouts of environmental investigation than after ground-level female marks. This response occurred across the age-sex categories, extending the effect beyond sampling at the scent location itself.

slides.title: Complementary methods distinguish natural scent mixtures
body: 'A **metabolome** is the collection of small chemical compounds in a sample. Hou and colleagues compared marked bark and nearby panda feces using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, or GC-MS, and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, or LC-MS. Both methods separated the chemical profiles of these materials.

GC-MS detected readily volatile molecules, compounds that enter the gas phase. LC-MS expanded the inventory to additional acids, heterocycles, and semi-volatile constituents. A heterocycle is a molecular ring containing an atom other than carbon. The methods therefore captured complementary components of the mixture.

Marked bark contained different chemistry from feces, including both airborne compounds and more strongly retained material. The authors proposed the hypothesis that microbes convert some retained constituents into odorants. This connects the immediate odor profile with a reservoir of material capable of changing after deposition.

slides.title: Scent-marked bark carries a distinct microbial community
body: A **microbiome** is the community of microorganisms associated with a habitat or host. Hou and colleagues compared bacteria in marked bark, nearby unmarked bark, and panda feces using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequences to classify bacterial groups.

Unmarked bark served as an environmental comparison for the surface before considering panda scent deposition. Marked bark and unmarked bark shared more community structure than either shared with feces, while marking was associated with changes in community diversity.

This pattern places scent material within an existing environmental microbial habitat. The mark is sampled and modified on bark rather than in a sterile container. Microbial community differences provide candidate biological processes through which a deposited chemical mixture can change as it remains at a communication site.

This pattern places scent material within an existing environmental microbial habitat. The mark is sampled and modified on bark rather than in a sterile container. Microbial community differences provide candidate biological processes through which a deposited chemical mixture can change as it remains at a communication site.

slides.title: Marked bark and feces support different bacterial groups
body: A **bacterial phylum** is a broad taxonomic group containing related bacterial lineages. Hou and colleagues characterized the prominent phyla in marked bark, unmarked bark, and feces, linking community composition with the chemical material sampled.

Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Bacteroidetes were prominent at scent-marking sites. Feces also contained abundant Proteobacteria and Bacteroidetes but included Firmicutes among its dominant groups. Similar broad categories can coexist with different relative compositions and finer-scale lineages.

The fecal community reflects a different biological substrate from the tree surface. Marked bark combines environmental microbes with animal-derived material, while feces carry the products of intestinal processing. These community differences accompany distinct metabolite profiles and support examining each substrate separately when investigating panda chemical communication.

slides.title: Enriched bacteria distinguish scent sites from controls
body: An **enriched taxon** is a biological group that is more abundant in one sample category than in comparison categories. Hou and colleagues identified bacterial groups associated with marked bark, unmarked bark, and feces.

These taxa provide candidates for studying chemical transformations at marking sites. The authors connected microbial composition with measured metabolites rather than assuming that every bacterium found on bark produces a social signal. The coexistence of different bacteria and compounds supplies a biological context for experiments on how the composition of a scent changes after deposition.

body: A **bacterial genus** groups closely related bacterial species. Hou and colleagues compared bacterial genera with volatile compounds measured at scent-marking sites, searching for coordinated variation across samples.

Ahniella was positively associated with vanillin and negatively associated with nonanal. Collimonas showed positive associations with several compounds, including decanal. These relationships connect particular components of the microbial community with particular components of the odor mixture.

The **fermentation hypothesis** proposes that microorganisms convert deposited material into odor compounds used in communication. The observed associations supply candidates for this hypothesis, rather than identifying each microbial reaction directly. Their direction and specificity narrow the combinations of bacteria and chemicals that can be tested experimentally for scent production.

slides.title: Steroid-related metabolites extend the scent substrate
body: A **steroid** is a molecule with a characteristic four-ring carbon framework. LC-MS measurements of marked bark included steroid-related compounds in addition to the more readily volatile compounds captured by GC-MS.

Several bacterial genera covaried with these metabolites. Brevundimonas had positive associations with compounds including epitestosterone and 6β-hydroxycortisol. These observations locate reproductive and metabolic chemistry within the environmental material deposited at a scent site.

The authors proposed the hypothesis that microbes transform some relatively odorless compounds into more odorous derivatives. Such conversion would connect physiological material from the sender with the chemistry available to a receiver after deposition. Measuring the metabolites and their microbial associations establishes candidate substrates for testing that proposed transformation.

slides.title: Scent identity depends on mixtures and their environment
body: A **chemical profile** is the combination of compounds present in a sample and their relative representation. Wild panda marks contain multiple odorants, environmental constituents, and material associated with bacterial communities.

The individual-discrimination experiment establishes that male gland profiles differ in ways pandas can perceive. The genomic study identifies a diverse receptor repertoire, while field chemistry supplies candidate molecules such as nonanal and decanal within natural marking substrates.

These findings connect three levels of chemical communication: a deposited mixture, a sensory molecular inventory, and a measurable receiver response. The hypothesis that a particular compound-receptor combination accounts for donor identity requires direct testing. Existing behavioral discrimination is compatible with information carried by a combination of compounds rather than a single universal identity molecule.

slides.title: The estrogen peak anchors the timing of estrus
body: **Estrus** is the period of female sexual receptivity associated with the reproductive cycle. Lindburg and colleagues measured urinary estrogen and behavior in the same female over three spring mating seasons, aligning daily observations to the estrogen peak.

The major urinary estrogen measured was estrone sulfate, with concentrations expressed relative to urinary creatinine. Creatinine normalization reduces variation caused by urine dilution. Values rose from below 50 ng/mg creatinine to above 600 ng/mg, then declined over approximately two days.

Artificial insemination after the peak produced a pregnancy and live cub in the final season. The rapid decline and concurrent behavioral changes therefore located a fertile interval near ovulation. Hormonal measurements provide a temporal reference against which distinct courtship behaviors can be compared.

slides.title: Female scent marking rises before the estrogen maximum
body: Female **scent-marking rate** changed markedly during the spring reproductive cycle. Outside the presumed estrous periods, the observed female averaged fewer than two marks per hour. During reproductive activity, marking sometimes approached 50 marks per hour.

Marking began to rise before a clear increase in urinary estrogen, reached high levels during the early estrogen ascent, and declined before the hormone maximum. Its timing therefore differed from a response that simply increases in parallel with the current estrogen concentration.

By the day after the estrogen peak, marking had returned near baseline while other reproductive behaviors remained active. The sequence shifts the female's communication from extensive early chemical deposition toward behaviors concentrated around the fertile interval. Courtship signaling changes its form as the reproductive state progresses.

slides.title: Bleating peaks after estrogen begins to decline
body: A **bleat** is a vocal signal associated with friendly or solicitous interactions in pandas. In the observed female, bleating occurred at low rates outside estrus and increased several days before the estrogen peak.

Bleating reached approximately 60 calls per hour on the day after the estrogen maximum. It remained elevated after estrogen had returned toward baseline. Scent marking, by contrast, had already declined sharply by this stage.

The authors proposed a **triggering hypothesis**: rising estrogen initiates a sequence of behavioral changes whose continued expression need not track the hormone's moment-to-moment concentration. Different timings of marking and bleating fit a staged reproductive sequence, with early surface signaling followed by more frequent vocal interaction near the fertile period.

slides.title: Tail-up and rear presentation cluster near ovulation
body: The **tail-up display** raises the tail during reproductive behavior. **Rear presentation** occurs when the female positions her hindquarters toward a male, sometimes adopting lordosis, an arched posture associated with receptivity.

In Lindburg and colleagues' observations, rear presentation became more common before the estrogen peak. Presentations accompanied by tail-up or lordosis were concentrated from one day before to three days after the peak, and touching the tail base could induce tail-up during this interval.

Tail-up occurred even after estrogen concentrations had declined. The combination of behavioral changes and the hormonal trajectory therefore provided a better description of the fertile interval than hormone concentration alone. The sender's reproductive state was expressed through posture, vocalization, and chemical deposition on different time courses.

slides.title: Female mate preference predicts successful mating
body: **Mate preference** is differential behavior toward potential partners. Martin-Wintle and colleagues tested a female's responses to two neighboring males before a mating introduction, measuring positive sexual behaviors and time spent near the candidates.

The candidates were genetically suitable partners, and barred windows permitted visual, vocal, and olfactory interaction while limiting physical contact. Preference was assessed before the animals were paired for mating, separating the behavioral predictor from the later reproductive outcome.

Females paired with preferred males had more successful intromissions, meaning penetration during copulation, and more cub production after mating. Preference therefore related both to participation in mating and to subsequent reproductive success. The result connects sensory and social assessment before contact with the outcome of a breeding introduction.

slides.title: Male mate preference also predicts reproductive outcomes
body: Male pandas also expressed **mate preferences** in the pre-introduction tests. The investigators applied the behavioral assessment to males as well as females, allowing reproductive outcomes to be related to each partner's choice.

Males paired with preferred females achieved more successful intromissions and produced more cubs than males paired with non-preferred females. Prior successful reproduction with a partner and male body mass also contributed to aspects of reproductive performance.

Male assessment therefore forms part of the reproductive interaction rather than merely responding to any receptive female. A female's willingness to approach a male and that male's response to her can vary independently. Evaluating both partners connects the sensory and behavioral preparation for mating with the mutual coordination required for successful copulation.

slides.title: Mutual preference is associated with the strongest breeding
body: **Mutual preference** occurs when both partners prefer one another. Martin-Wintle and colleagues separated pairings into four combinations: both preferred, only the female preferred, only the male preferred, or neither preferred.

Successful intromission occurred in approximately 83% of mutually preferred pairings, whereas none occurred in pairings where neither animal preferred the other. Pairings with preference on only one side had intermediate mating performance.

Cub production also favored mutually preferred pairings. Its denominator differs from the full pairing rate in the source, because cub production is evaluated after successful mating. The pattern connects reciprocal social assessment with coordinated reproductive behavior, while keeping the successive stages of pairing, copulation, and offspring production conceptually distinct.

slides.title: Genetic suitability can coexist with behavioral choice
body: **Genetic suitability** concerns avoiding close inbreeding and maintaining genetic representation in a breeding population. **Behavioral compatibility** concerns whether the animals interact in ways that permit mating. The panda preference tests considered choice among already suitable candidate partners.

Preference information improved prediction of mating outcomes, while the hormone-behavior study located the short reproductive interval. These observations concern different parts of reproduction: the partner selected and the timing at which the female is receptive.

Chemical communication contributes additional information before direct encounter, through deposited marks and active investigation. Combining candidate suitability, reciprocal preference, and reproductive timing permits breeding decisions to incorporate the animal's sensory and behavioral biology. The studies connect managed introductions with processes already present in the panda's communication system.
